[[:db/retract 17592186152483 :question/answer-fields 17592186149472] [:db/retract 17592186152486 :question/answer-fields 17592186149485] {:db/id 17592186152090 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-99665861-b940-5f61-80d5-9c97648d3f5e" "question-40d1d6db-2cfa-5253-ab0a-58b0f4105c36" "question-82ba7d3c-5902-5665-8148-515fc5c0a008" "question-eca33d65-a659-5a03-8cda-7de1fade1db7" "question-11d5fb97-c633-54cb-abf0-947c2b0b0a09"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151856 :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $3x \equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\,20)?$ 

- $x  \equiv 5 \quad  (\textrm{mod}\,20)$

- $x  \equiv 7 \quad  (\textrm{mod}\,20)$

- $x  \equiv 9 \quad  (\textrm{mod}\,20)$" :question/worked-solution "The scalar multiplication properties of congruences state that for $k \in \mathbb{Z},$ we have the following:

- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$

- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,kn)$

The modulus equals $20$ in all statements, which suggests we'll need to use the first property.

Notice that the coefficient of $x$ is $3,$ and $7\cdot 3 = 21$ is one larger than the modulus. Therefore, we can reduce the coefficient of $x$ to unity as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ 7\cdot 3x & ≡7\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ 21x & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ x+20x & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ x+0x & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ x & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,20)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
3x \equiv 1  \quad \Longrightarrow \quad 
x \equiv 7\qquad  (\textrm{mod}\,20)
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152091 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e40b6e95-46c9-501b-9cf3-a3ca43d4de46" "question-6f365d70-97c4-5d2a-be4d-f7de85215156" "question-4a7e58ae-7402-5947-902d-187649afe03f" "question-33e605f0-847a-5675-b130-592bda56586a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151840 :question/problem "Use the multiplicative property of congruences to compute the residue of $76 \cdot 122 \textrm{ mod } 6.$" :question/worked-solution "The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}76 & ≡12\cdot 6+4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡12\cdot 0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ 122 & ≡20\cdot 6+2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡20\cdot 0+2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}76\cdot 122 & ≡4\cdot 2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡6+2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡0+2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
76 \cdot 122 \equiv 2 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,6).
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152092 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d32d1e8e-c6cb-5e8e-ad44-72ef38726d73" "question-d8e0aa45-c7f0-5602-aeab-6e88c994c623" "question-cc39a9be-d29f-5f9f-ba0f-0e6107657cab" "question-ca2a2b4b-a4c2-5e49-b032-7cf6b84669a2" "question-a3bd2c71-c0a1-5bcf-99be-f98d89cf7b38"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151841 :question/problem "Use the multiplicative property of congruences to compute the residue of $5^{7} \textrm{ mod } 8.$" :question/worked-solution "The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

$$
5^{7} = 5^2\cdot 5^2 \cdot 5^3.
$$

Next, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{2} & ≡25\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡3\cdot 8+1\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡3\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\ {5}^{3} & ≡5\cdot {5}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡5\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{7} & ≡{5}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}\cdot {5}^{3}\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡1\cdot 1\cdot 5\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
5^{7} \textrm{ mod } 8= 5.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152093 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6f6da8c7-058a-5fb2-9ce1-1161fee7e94e" "question-42a09307-b06f-57dd-a795-e7f9c01844a8" "question-b06970b0-8be9-550a-81a5-76772304b000" "question-838b9afb-8969-5aff-9073-fc6f44eddea1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151864 :question/problem "What is the last digit in the decimal expansion of $17^{13}?$" :question/worked-solution "If $a\equiv b\:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$ and $c\equiv d\:(\textrm{mod}\,n),$ then the following properties hold:

- $ac\equiv bd  \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$

- $a^k \equiv b^k  \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$ for any positive integer $k$

To find the last digit, we need to calculate the following residue:

$$
17^{13} \textrm{ mod } 10
$$

First, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}17 & ≡10+7\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡0+7\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the exponentiation property, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{17}^{2} & ≡{7}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡49\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡4\cdot 10+9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡4\cdot 0+9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\ {17}^{4} & ≡{9}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡81\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡8\cdot 10+1\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡8\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we decompose $17^{13}$ into a product of smaller exponents. 

$$
17^{13} =  \left(17^4\right)^3\cdot 17
$$

By applying the multiplicative and exponentiation properties, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{17}^{13} & ≡{({17}^{4})}^{3}\cdot 17\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡(1)^{3}\cdot 7\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡1\cdot 7\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
17^{13} \textrm{ mod } 10 = 7
$$

which means that the last digit of $17^{13}$ is $7.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-99665861-b940-5f61-80d5-9c97648d3f5e" :question/id #uuid "99665861-b940-5f61-80d5-9c97648d3f5e" :question/math-academy-id "q-213133" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $2x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,15)?$" :question/worked-solution "The scalar multiplication properties of congruences state that for $k\in Z,$ we have the following:

The modulus equals $15$ in all statements, which suggests we'll need to use the first property.

Notice that the coefficient of $x$ is $2,$ and $8\cdot 2=16$ is one larger than the modulus. Therefore, we can reduce the coefficient of $x$ to unity as follows:

\begin{aligned}2x & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ 8\cdot 2x & ≡8\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ 16x & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+15x & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+0x & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}

17592186153451 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the modular congruence

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

One useful property of congruences is that we can *multiply* both sides by an *integer*, similar to regular equations.

For example, consider the true statement

$$
7\equiv 2 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5).
$$

Multiplying both sides by (for example) $9$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}9\cdot 7 & ≡9\cdot 2\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 63 & ≡18\, & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement since $63$ and $18$ both have a remainder of $3$ when divided by $5.$

In general, the **scalar multiplication property** of congruences states that for $k\in\mathbb{Z},$

$$
a\equiv b  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

We also have

$$
a\equiv b  \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,kn).
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153463 :tutorial/content "Another useful property that stems from the multiplication property is as follows. Suppose that 

$$
a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

Using this, we can compute the residue of a large product without finding the product explicitly. Let's see how." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153469 :tutorial/content "The multiplicative property states that given $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$ and $c \equiv d \: (\textrm{mod}\,n),$ we obtain $ac \equiv bd \: (\textrm{mod}\,n).$ By taking the same congruence twice, we obtain 

$$
a^2 \equiv b^2  \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

In general, 

$$
a^k \equiv b^k  \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

for any *positive* integer $k.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153473 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've made use of the following properties:

- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$

- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,kn)$

Let's prove the first property. The proof of the second property is similar.

It's straightforward to prove the scalar multiplication property from the definition of congruence. First, note that we have the following chain of implications for $k, p\in\mathbb Z$:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\, & ⟹\,a-b=pn \\  & ⟹\,k(a-b)=kpn \\  & ⟹\,ka-kb=(kp)n\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $kp = q\in\mathbb Z.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ka-kb=(kp)n\, & ⟹\,ka-kb=qn \\  & ⟹\,ka≡kb\,(\text{mod}\,n).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

Note the following:

- The proof of the second property is very similar.

- We'll prove the multiplicative and exponentiation properties in future lessons." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152341 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

- $x  \equiv 5 \quad  (\textrm{mod}\,20)$

- $x  \equiv 7 \quad  (\textrm{mod}\,20)$

- $x  \equiv 9 \quad  (\textrm{mod}\,20)$" :question/worked-solution "The scalar multiplication properties of congruences state that for $k \in \mathbb{Z},$ we have the following:

- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$

- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,kn)$

The modulus equals $20$ in all statements, which suggests we'll need to use the first property.

Notice that the coefficient of $x$ is $3,$ and $7\cdot 3 = 21$ is one larger than the modulus. Therefore, we can reduce the coefficient of $x$ to unity as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ 7\cdot 3x & ≡7\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ 21x & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ x+20x & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ x+0x & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ x & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,20)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
3x \equiv 1  \quad \Longrightarrow \quad 
x \equiv 7\qquad  (\textrm{mod}\,20)
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152091 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e40b6e95-46c9-501b-9cf3-a3ca43d4de46" "question-6f365d70-97c4-5d2a-be4d-f7de85215156" "question-4a7e58ae-7402-5947-902d-187649afe03f" "question-33e605f0-847a-5675-b130-592bda56586a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151840 :question/problem "Use the multiplicative property of congruences to compute the residue of $76 \cdot 122 \textrm{ mod } 6.$" :question/worked-solution "The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}76 & ≡12\cdot 6+4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡12\cdot 0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ 122 & ≡20\cdot 6+2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡20\cdot 0+2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}76\cdot 122 & ≡4\cdot 2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡6+2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡0+2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
76 \cdot 122 \equiv 2 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,6).
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152092 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d32d1e8e-c6cb-5e8e-ad44-72ef38726d73" "question-d8e0aa45-c7f0-5602-aeab-6e88c994c623" "question-cc39a9be-d29f-5f9f-ba0f-0e6107657cab" "question-ca2a2b4b-a4c2-5e49-b032-7cf6b84669a2" "question-a3bd2c71-c0a1-5bcf-99be-f98d89cf7b38"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151841 :question/problem "Use the multiplicative property of congruences to compute the residue of $5^{7} \textrm{ mod } 8.$" :question/worked-solution "The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

$$
5^{7} = 5^2\cdot 5^2 \cdot 5^3.
$$

Next, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{2} & ≡25\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡3\cdot 8+1\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡3\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\ {5}^{3} & ≡5\cdot {5}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡5\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{7} & ≡{5}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}\cdot {5}^{3}\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡1\cdot 1\cdot 5\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
5^{7} \textrm{ mod } 8= 5.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152093 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6f6da8c7-058a-5fb2-9ce1-1161fee7e94e" "question-42a09307-b06f-57dd-a795-e7f9c01844a8" "question-b06970b0-8be9-550a-81a5-76772304b000" "question-838b9afb-8969-5aff-9073-fc6f44eddea1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151864 :question/problem "What is the last digit in the decimal expansion of $17^{13}?$" :question/worked-solution "If $a\equiv b\:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$ and $c\equiv d\:(\textrm{mod}\,n),$ then the following properties hold:

- $ac\equiv bd  \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$

- $a^k \equiv b^k  \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$ for any positive integer $k$

To find the last digit, we need to calculate the following residue:

$$
17^{13} \textrm{ mod } 10
$$

First, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}17 & ≡10+7\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡0+7\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the exponentiation property, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{17}^{2} & ≡{7}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡49\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡4\cdot 10+9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡4\cdot 0+9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\ {17}^{4} & ≡{9}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡81\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡8\cdot 10+1\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡8\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we decompose $17^{13}$ into a product of smaller exponents. 

$$
17^{13} =  \left(17^4\right)^3\cdot 17
$$

By applying the multiplicative and exponentiation properties, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{17}^{13} & ≡{({17}^{4})}^{3}\cdot 17\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡(1)^{3}\cdot 7\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡1\cdot 7\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
17^{13} \textrm{ mod } 10 = 7
$$

which means that the last digit of $17^{13}$ is $7.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-99665861-b940-5f61-80d5-9c97648d3f5e" :question/id #uuid "99665861-b940-5f61-80d5-9c97648d3f5e" :question/math-academy-id "q-213133" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $2x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,15)?$" :question/worked-solution "The scalar multiplication properties of congruences state that for $k\in Z,$ we have the following:

- $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\,⟹\,ka≡kb\,(\text{mod}\,n)$

- $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\,⟹\,ka≡kb\,(\text{mod}\,kn)$

The modulus equals $15$ in all statements, which suggests we'll need to use the first property.

Notice that the coefficient of $x$ is $2,$ and $8\cdot 2=16$ is one larger than the modulus. Therefore, we can reduce the coefficient of $x$ to unity as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ 8\cdot 2x & ≡8\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ 16x & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+15x & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+0x & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}

- $ac≡bd\,(\text{mod}\,n)$

- ${a}^{k}≡{b}^{k}\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ for any positive integer $k$

To find the last digit, we need to calculate the following residue:

$$
{28}^{18}\text{ mod }10
$$

First, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}28 & ≡20+8\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡2\cdot 10+8\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡2\cdot 0+8\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the exponentiation property, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{28}^{2} & ≡{8}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡64\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡6\cdot 10+4\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡6\cdot 0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\ {28}^{6} & ≡{({28}^{2})}^{3}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡{4}^{3}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡64\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡6\cdot 10+4 & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡6\cdot 0+4 & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we decompose ${28}^{18}$ into a product of smaller exponents. 

$$
{28}^{18}={({28}^{6})}^{3}
$$

By applying the multiplicative and exponentiation properties, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{28}^{18} & ≡{({28}^{6})}^{3}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡(4)^{3}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡64\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡6\cdot 10+4\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡6\cdot 0+4 & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{28}^{18}\text{ mod }10=4
$$

which means that the last digit of ${28}^{18}$ is $4.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b24580b0-549e-52ef-8518-91948f4e984f"] :db/ensure $$

$$
{29}^{13}\text{ mod }10
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}29 & ≡20+9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡2\cdot 10+9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡2\cdot 0+9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{29}^{2} & ≡{9}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡81\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡8\cdot 10+1\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡8\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we decompose ${29}^{13}$ into a product of smaller exponents. 

$$
{29}^{13}={({29}^{2})}^{6}\cdot 29
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{29}^{13} & ≡{({29}^{2})}^{6}\cdot 29\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡(1)^{6}\cdot 9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡1\cdot 9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}

$$

17592186153451 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the modular congruence

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

One useful property of congruences is that we can *multiply* both sides by an *integer*, similar to regular equations.

For example, consider the true statement

$$
7\equiv 2 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5).
$$

Multiplying both sides by (for example) $9$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}9\cdot 7 & ≡9\cdot 2\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 63 & ≡18\, & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement since $63$ and $18$ both have a remainder of $3$ when divided by $5.$

In general, the **scalar multiplication property** of congruences states that for $k\in\mathbb{Z},$

$$
a\equiv b  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

We also have

$$
a\equiv b  \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,kn).
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153463 :tutorial/content "Another useful property that stems from the multiplication property is as follows. Suppose that 

$$
a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

Using this, we can compute the residue of a large product without finding the product explicitly. Let's see how." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153469 :tutorial/content "The multiplicative property states that given $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$ and $c \equiv d \: (\textrm{mod}\,n),$ we obtain $ac \equiv bd \: (\textrm{mod}\,n).$ By taking the same congruence twice, we obtain 

$$
a^2 \equiv b^2  \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

In general, 

$$
a^k \equiv b^k  \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

for any *positive* integer $k.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153473 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've made use of the following properties:

- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$

- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,kn)$

Let's prove the first property. The proof of the second property is similar.

It's straightforward to prove the scalar multiplication property from the definition of congruence. First, note that we have the following chain of implications for $k, p\in\mathbb Z$:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\, & ⟹\,a-b=pn \\  & ⟹\,k(a-b)=kpn \\  & ⟹\,ka-kb=(kp)n\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $kp = q\in\mathbb Z.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ka-kb=(kp)n\, & ⟹\,ka-kb=qn \\  & ⟹\,ka≡kb\,(\text{mod}\,n).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

Note the following:

- The proof of the second property is very similar.

- We'll prove the multiplicative and exponentiation properties in future lessons." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152341 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186151856 :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $3x \equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\,20)?$ 

- $x  \equiv 5 \quad  (\textrm{mod}\,20)$

- $x  \equiv 7 \quad  (\textrm{mod}\,20)$

- $x  \equiv 9 \quad  (\textrm{mod}\,20)$"] [17592186151856 :question/worked-solution "The scalar multiplication properties of congruences state that for $k \in \mathbb{Z},$ we have the following:

- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$

- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,kn)$

The modulus equals $20$ in all statements, which suggests we'll need to use the first property.

Notice that the coefficient of $x$ is $3,$ and $7\cdot 3 = 21$ is one larger than the modulus. Therefore, we can reduce the coefficient of $x$ to unity as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ 7\cdot 3x & ≡7\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ 21x & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ x+20x & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ x+0x & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ x & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,20)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
3x \equiv 1  \quad \Longrightarrow \quad 
x \equiv 7\qquad  (\textrm{mod}\,20)
$$"] [17592186151840 :question/problem "Use the multiplicative property of congruences to compute the residue of $76 \cdot 122 \textrm{ mod } 6.$"] [17592186151840 :question/worked-solution "The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}76 & ≡12\cdot 6+4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡12\cdot 0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ 122 & ≡20\cdot 6+2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡20\cdot 0+2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}76\cdot 122 & ≡4\cdot 2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡6+2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡0+2\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
76 \cdot 122 \equiv 2 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,6).
$$"] [17592186151841 :question/problem "Use the multiplicative property of congruences to compute the residue of $5^{7} \textrm{ mod } 8.$"] [17592186151841 :question/worked-solution "The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

$$
5^{7} = 5^2\cdot 5^2 \cdot 5^3.
$$

Next, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{2} & ≡25\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡3\cdot 8+1\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡3\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\ {5}^{3} & ≡5\cdot {5}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡5\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{7} & ≡{5}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}\cdot {5}^{3}\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡1\cdot 1\cdot 5\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
5^{7} \textrm{ mod } 8= 5.
$$"] [17592186151864 :question/problem "What is the last digit in the decimal expansion of $17^{13}?$"] [17592186151864 :question/worked-solution "If $a\equiv b\:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$ and $c\equiv d\:(\textrm{mod}\,n),$ then the following properties hold:

- $ac\equiv bd  \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$

- $a^k \equiv b^k  \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$ for any positive integer $k$

To find the last digit, we need to calculate the following residue:

$$
17^{13} \textrm{ mod } 10
$$

First, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}17 & ≡10+7\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡0+7\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the exponentiation property, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{17}^{2} & ≡{7}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡49\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡4\cdot 10+9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡4\cdot 0+9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\ {17}^{4} & ≡{9}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡81\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡8\cdot 10+1\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡8\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we decompose $17^{13}$ into a product of smaller exponents. 

$$
17^{13} =  \left(17^4\right)^3\cdot 17
$$

By applying the multiplicative and exponentiation properties, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{17}^{13} & ≡{({17}^{4})}^{3}\cdot 17\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡(1)^{3}\cdot 7\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡1\cdot 7\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡7\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
17^{13} \textrm{ mod } 10 = 7
$$

which means that the last digit of $17^{13}$ is $7.$"] ["question-99665861-b940-5f61-80d5-9c97648d3f5e" :question/id #uuid "99665861-b940-5f61-80d5-9c97648d3f5e"] ["question-99665861-b940-5f61-80d5-9c97648d3f5e" :question/math-academy-id "q-213133"] ["question-99665861-b940-5f61-80d5-9c97648d3f5e" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $2x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,15)?$"] ["question-99665861-b940-5f61-80d5-9c97648d3f5e" :question/worked-solution "The scalar multiplication properties of congruences state that for $k\in Z,$ we have the following:

:question/problem "By the multiplicative property of congruences, ${20}^{4}≡$"] ["question-d8e0aa45-c7f0-5602-aeab-6e88c994c623" :question/worked-solution "The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a≡b\,\text{and}\,c≡d\,(\text{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac≡bd\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

$$
{20}^{4}=(4\cdot 5)^{4}={4}^{2}\cdot {4}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}.
$$

Next, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{2} & ≡16\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡2\cdot 6+4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡2\cdot 0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ {5}^{2} & ≡25\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡4\cdot 6+1\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡4\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{20}^{4} & ≡{4}^{2}\cdot {4}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡4\cdot 4\cdot 1\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡16\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡2\cdot 6+4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡2\cdot 0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{20}^{4}≡4\,\,(\text{mod}\,6).
$$"] ["question-d8e0aa45-c7f0-5602-aeab-6e88c994c623" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-0588c800-d87c-56d9-83a6-8993a8964638" :answer-field/id #uuid congruences states that if

$$
a≡b\,\text{and}\,c≡d\,(\text{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac≡bd\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

$$
{6}^{6}={6}^{2}\cdot {6}^{2}\cdot {6}^{2}.
$$

Next, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{6}^{2} & ≡36\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡4\cdot 8+4\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡4\cdot 0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{6}^{6} & ≡{6}^{2}\cdot {6}^{2}\cdot {6}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡4\cdot 4\cdot 4\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡64\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡8\cdot 8+0\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡8\cdot 0+0\, & (\text{mod}\,8) \\  & ≡0\, & (\text{mod}\,8)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{6}^{6}≡0\,\,(\text{mod}\,8).
$$"] ["question-cc39a9be-d29f-5f9f-ba0f-0e6107657cab" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-73c85ead-eecb-5b52-b908-fbc0204c2c1e" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "By the multiplicative property of congruences, ${12}^{6}≡$"] ["question-ca2a2b4b-a4c2-5e49-b032-7cf6b84669a2" :question/worked-solution "The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a≡b\,\text{and}\,c≡d\,(\text{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac≡bd\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

$$
{12}^{6}=(3\cdot 4)^{6}={3}^{3}\cdot {3}^{3}\cdot {4}^{3}\cdot {4}^{3}.
$$

Next, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{3} & ≡27\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡3\cdot 9+0\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡3\cdot 0+0\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡0\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ {4}^{3} & ≡64\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡7\cdot 9+1\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡7\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{12}^{6} & ≡{3}^{3}\cdot {3}^{3}\cdot {4}^{3}\cdot {4}^{3}\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡0\cdot 0\cdot 1\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡0\, & (\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{12}^{6}≡0\,\,(\text{mod}\,9).

{{field-1}}"] ["question-a3bd2c71-c0a1-5bcf-99be-f98d89cf7b38" :question/worked-solution "The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a≡b\,\text{and}\,c≡d\,(\text{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac≡bd\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

$$
{8}^{6}={8}^{2}\cdot {8}^{2}\cdot {8}^{2}.
$$

Next, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{2} & ≡64\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡7\cdot 9+1\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡7\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{6} & ≡{8}^{2}\cdot {8}^{2}\cdot {8}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡1\cdot 1\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,9) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{8}^{6}\,\,\text{mod}\,9=1.
$$"] ["question-a3bd2c71-c0a1-5bcf-99be-f98d89cf7b38" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-52eefa79-7a00-5342-a326-3242d4e53917" :answer-field/id #uuid "52eefa79-7a00-5342-a326-3242d4e53917"] ["answer-5ecf2566-0fbb-5c3c-bd2b-a10c6c13ce83" :answer/id #uuid "5ecf2566-0fbb-5c3c-bd2b-a10c6c13ce83"] ["answer-5ecf2566-0fbb-5c3c-bd2b-a10c6c13ce83" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-5ecf2566-0fbb-5c3c-bd2b-a10c6c13ce83" :answer/value "1"] ["answer-field-52eefa79-7a00-5342-a326-3242d4e53917" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-52eefa79-7a00-5342-a326-3242d4e53917" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-52eefa79-7a00-5342-a326-3242d4e53917" :answer-field/correct "answer-5ecf2566-0fbb-5c3c-bd2b-a10c6c13ce83"] ["answer-field-52eefa79-7a00-5342-a326-3242d4e53917" :answer-field/choices "answer-5ecf2566-0fbb-5c3c-bd2b-a10c6c13ce83"] ["question-a3bd2c71-c0a1-5bcf-99be-f98d89cf7b38" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-52eefa79-7a00-5342-a326-3242d4e53917"] [17592186152092 :knowledge-point/questions "question-a3bd2c71-c0a1-5bcf-99be-f98d89cf7b38"] ["question-6f6da8c7-058a-5fb2-9ce1-1161fee7e94e" :question/id #uuid "6f6da8c7-058a-5fb2-9ce1-1161fee7e94e"] ["question-6f6da8c7-058a-5fb2-9ce1-1161fee7e94e" :question/math-academy-id "q-213171"] ["question-6f6da8c7-058a-5fb2-9ce1-1161fee7e94e" :question/problem "What is the last digit in the decimal expansion of ${28}^{18}?$"] ["question-6f6da8c7-058a-5fb2-9ce1-1161fee7e94e" :question/worked-solution "If $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ and $c≡d\,(\text{mod}\,n),$ then the following properties hold:

expansion of ${13}^{13}?$"] ["question-838b9afb-8969-5aff-9073-fc6f44eddea1" :question/worked-solution "If $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ and $c≡d\,(\text{mod}\,n),$ then the following properties hold:

- $ac≡bd\,(\text{mod}\,n)$

- ${a}^{k}≡{b}^{k}\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ for any positive integer $k$

To find the last digit, we need to calculate the following residue:

$$
{13}^{13}\text{ mod }10
$$

First, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}13 & ≡10+3\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡0+3\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡3\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the exponentiation property, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{13}^{4} & ≡{3}^{4}\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡81\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡8\cdot 10+1\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡8\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we decompose ${13}^{13}$ into a product of smaller exponents. 

$$
{13}^{13}={({13}^{4})}^{3}\cdot 13
$$

By applying the multiplicative and exponentiation properties, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{13}^{13} & ≡{({13}^{4})}^{3}\cdot 13\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡(1)^{3}\cdot 3\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡1\cdot 3\, & (\text{mod}\,10) \\  & ≡3\, & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{13}^{13}\text{ mod }10=3
$$

which means that the last digit of ${13}^{13}$ is $3.$"] ["question-838b9afb-8969-5aff-9073-fc6f44eddea1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] "question-11d5fb97-c633-54cb-abf0-947c2b0b0a09"] [17592186153451 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the modular congruence

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

One useful property of congruences is that we can *multiply* both sides by an *integer*, similar to regular equations.

For example, consider the true statement

$$
7\equiv 2 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5).
$$

Multiplying both sides by (for example) $9$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}9\cdot 7 & ≡9\cdot 2\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 63 & ≡18\, & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement since $63$ and $18$ both have a remainder of $3$ when divided by $5.$

In general, the **scalar multiplication property** of congruences states that for $k\in\mathbb{Z},$

$$
a\equiv b  \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

We also have

$$
a\equiv b  \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,kn).

To find the last digit, we need to calculate the following residue:
$17^{13} \textrm{mod} 10$

First, we note the following:

$$
17 \mid ≡10 + 7\begin{vmatrix}(mod10) \\ ≡0 + 7\end{vmatrix}(mod10); ≡7 \mid (mod10)
$$

Therefore, by the exponentiation property, we have the following:

$$
17^{2}\begin{vmatrix}≡7^{2} & (mod10) \\ ≡49 & (mod10) \\ ≡4 \cdot 10 + 9 & (mod10) \\ ≡4 \cdot 0 + 9 & (mod10) \\ ≡9 & (mod10) \\ 17^{4} & ≡9^{2}\end{vmatrix}(mod10); ≡81\begin{vmatrix}(mod10) \\ ≡8 \cdot 10 + 1\end{vmatrix}(mod10); ≡8 \cdot 0 + 1\begin{vmatrix}(mod10) \\ ≡1\end{vmatrix}(mod10)
$$

Next, we decompose $17^{13}$ into a product of smaller exponents.

$$
17^{13} = \left(17^4\right)^3\cdot 17
$$

By applying the multiplicative and exponentiation properties, we have the following:

$$
17^{13} \mid ≡(17^{4})^{3} \cdot 17\begin{vmatrix}(mod10) \\ ≡(1)^{3} \cdot 7\end{vmatrix}(mod10); ≡1 \cdot 7\begin{vmatrix}(mod10) \\ ≡7\end{vmatrix}(mod10)
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
17^{13} \textrm{mod} 10 = 7
$$

congruence

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

One useful property of congruences is that we can *multiply* both sides by an *integer*, similar to regular equations.

For example, consider the true statement

$$
7\equiv 2 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)
$$

Multiplying both sides by (for example) $9$ gives

$$
\begin{bmatrix}9 \cdot 7 & ≡9 \cdot 2 & (mod5) \\ 63 & ≡18 & (mod5)\end{bmatrix}
$$

which is a true statement since $63$ and $18$ both have a remainder of $3$ when divided by $5$.

In general, the **scalar multiplication property** of congruences states that for $k\in\mathbb{Z}$,

$$
a\equiv b \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

We also have

$$
a\equiv b \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,kn)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a3e0278c-44da-546e-bc47-9529380f4b5e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9017 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "150a8841-cd4a-55a0-9103-03b339daec90" :step/math-academy-id 154615 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152950}} {:db/id 17592186152950 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152090 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151856 :question/id #uuid "aa58ae42-bdf6-5303-9c9c-2e20151f2ed8" :question/math-academy-id "e-14610"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e8c69963-858d-5527-a8dd-33a9e0070f91" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049004}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152475} {:db/id 17592186152487}] :knowledge-point/title "Using the Scalar Multiplication Property"} :step/id #uuid "eb1b2b70-7fdf-523c-bc68-d9bd60ecf54c" :step/math-academy-id 154616 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152951}} {:db/id 17592186152951 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153463 :tutorial/content "Another useful property that stems from the multiplication property is as follows. for any *positive* integer $k$." :tutorial/id #uuid "a5dad198-84e6-5eab-9d7e-6df354768fce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9076 :tutorial/title "The Exponentiation Property"} :step/id #uuid "deefc65a-57e3-571f-a62b-93fbf75d0ee8" :step/math-academy-id 154627 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152955}} {:db/id 17592186152955 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152093 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151864 :question/id #uuid "21d3a5de-63f0-5150-9cb8-c2cbc609bb8b" :question/math-academy-id "e-14651"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "998b6175-c6d6-54a6-a970-003c6c85da7b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152486} {:db/id 17592186152488}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Final Digit"} :step/id #uuid "aaa53ec0-7f0e-5c35-81f0-63d71abae912" :step/math-academy-id 154628 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152956}} {:db/id 17592186152956 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153473 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've made use of the following properties:

- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$
- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,kn)$

Let's prove the first property. The proof of the second property is similar.

It's straightforward to prove the scalar multiplication property from the definition of congruence. First, note that we have the following chain of implications for $k, p\in\mathbb Z$:

$$
a≡b(modn) \mid ⟹a - b = pn; ⟹k(a - b) = kpn; ⟹ka - kb = (kp)n
$$

Now, let

$$
kp = q\in\mathbb Z
$$

Then, we have

$$
ka - kb = (kp)n \mid ⟹ka - kb = qn; ⟹ka≡kb(modn)
$$

Therefore, we conclude that
$a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$.

Note the following:

- The proof of the second property is very similar.
- We'll prove the multiplicative and exponentiation properties in future lessons." :tutorial/id #uuid "5cf4e7b1-34e6-55ea-bb8f-ae13a8fa29d3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9125 :tutorial/title "Proving the Scalar Multiplication Property"} :step/id #uuid "82d98a08-ff41-586d-97b2-d5622638b737" :step/math-academy-id 154631}] :activity/title "The Multiplication Properties of Modular Arithmetic" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186152341} {:db/id 17592186152949 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153451 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the modular congruence

a≡b(modn) \mid ⟹a - b = pn; ⟹k(a - b) = kpn; ⟹ka - kb = (kp)n
$$

Now, let

$$
kp = q\in\mathbb Z
$$

Then, we have

$$
ka - kb = (kp)n \mid ⟹ka - kb = qn; ⟹ka≡kb(modn)
$$

Therefore, we conclude that
$a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$.

Note the following:

- The proof of the second property is very similar.
- We'll prove the multiplicative and exponentiation properties in future lessons." :tutorial/id #uuid "5cf4e7b1-34e6-55ea-bb8f-ae13a8fa29d3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9125 :tutorial/title "Proving the By the end of the course, students will appreciate how set theory provides a comprehensive toolkit for proving mathematical results.
After mastering these fundamentals, students will explore various proof-writing techniques, including direct proof, proof by cases, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, disproof, and mathematical induction. Students will have multiple opportunities to test and refine their proof construction and comprehension skills throughout the course and in varied contexts

[17592186152956 1063 17592186153473 17592186045417] [17592186153451 1064 "Let's consider the modular congruence

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

One useful property of congruences is that we can *multiply* both sides by an *integer*, similar to regular equations.

For example, consider the true statement

$$
7\equiv 2 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)
$$

Multiplying both sides by (for example) $9$ gives

$$
\begin{bmatrix}9 \cdot 7 & ≡9 \cdot 2 & (mod5) \\ 63 & ≡18 & (mod5)\end{bmatrix}
$$

which is a true statement since $63$ and $18$ both have a remainder of $3$ when divided by $5$.

In general, the **scalar multiplication property** of congruences states that for $k\in\mathbb{Z}$,

$$
a\equiv b \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

We also have

$$
a\equiv b \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,kn)
$$" 17592186045417] [17592186153451 1065 9017 17592186045417] [17592186153451 1066 #uuid "a3e0278c-44da-546e-bc47-9529380f4b5e" 17592186045417] [17592186153451 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186153463 1064 "Another useful property that stems from the multiplication property is as follows. Suppose that

$$
a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

then, we have

$$
ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

Using this, we can compute the residue of a large product without finding the product explicitly. Let's see how." 17592186045417] [17592186153463 1065 9040 17592186045417] [17592186153463 1066 #uuid "5778b7fb-626e-59d3-ad81-8d574bb2b4e4" 17592186045417] [17592186153463 1067 "The Multiplicative Property" 17592186045417] [17592186153469 1064 "The multiplicative property states that given $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$ and $c \equiv d \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$, we obtain $ac \equiv bd \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$. By taking the same congruence twice, we obtain

$$
a^2 \equiv b^2 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

In general,

$$
a^k \equiv b^k \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

for any *positive* integer $k$." 17592186045417] [17592186153469 1065 9076 17592186045417] [17592186153469 1066 #uuid "a5dad198-84e6-5eab-9d7e-6df354768fce" 17592186045417] [17592186153469 1067 "The Exponentiation Property" 17592186045417] [17592186153473 1064 "Throughout this lesson, we've made use of the following properties:

- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$
- $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,kn)$

Let's prove the first property. The proof of the second property is similar.

It's straightforward to prove the scalar multiplication property from the definition of congruence. First, note that we have the following chain of implications for $k, p\in\mathbb Z$:

$$
a≡b(modn) \mid ⟹a - b = pn; ⟹k(a - b) = kpn; ⟹ka - kb = (kp)n
$$

Now, let

$$
kp = q\in\mathbb Z
$$

Then, we have

$$
ka - kb = (kp)n \mid ⟹ka - kb = qn; ⟹ka≡kb(modn)
$$

Therefore, we conclude that
$a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$.

Note the following:

- The proof of the second property is very similar.
- We'll prove the multiplicative and exponentiation properties in future lessons." 17592186045417] [17592186153473 1065 9125 17592186045417] [17592186153473 1066 #uuid "5cf4e7b1-34e6-55ea-bb8f-ae13a8fa29d3" 17592186045417] [17592186153473 1067 "Proving the Scalar Multiplication Property" 17592186045417]]}
